Speaker: Jason
Notes: Jason’s behavior towards his parents (after his father’s speech) can be interpreted as an expression of filial love (cf. 1.348-1.349).

Speaker: Aeson/Alcimede
Notes: Both Aeson and Alcimede are also described as worried and fearful before Cretheus’ speech (cf. 1.731 and 1.734).

Speaker: Lemnian women
Notes: Before Venus’ speech in 2.176-2.184, the text also refers to anger and sadness (cf. 2.165) as significant components of the women’s emotional states (alongside frenzy).

Speaker: Thoas
Notes: The god Bacchus is addressed here, but Thoas is present as audience.

Speaker: Hesione
Notes: After Hercules’ speech, Hesione also shows signs of fear and sadness (cf. 2.470).

Speaker: Cyzicans (Jason/Argonauts)
Notes: It is possible that the Argonauts’ fear (At Minyas anceps fixit pavor, V. Fl. 3.74, “But sudden fear paralyzed the Minyans”) also results from Pan’s utterance in 3.45 (for this discussion see Schirner 2023, 258-259 with further references). In this case, the Argonauts can also be interpreted as Pan’s audience.

Speaker: Jason/Argonauts
Notes: In my interpretation, vigiles … curas (V. Fl. 3.447, “vigilant … worries”) refers to the Argonauts and therefore can be analyzed as “audience’s emotion before the speech” (as the Argonauts are present during Mopsus’ expiation ritual).

Speaker: Telamon
Notes: After Meleager’s speech (3.649-3.689), Telamon is not only angry, but also surprised, sad, and grieving (cf. 3.692-3.695).

Speaker: Jason/Pollux/Argonauts
Notes: Some of the Argonauts are mentioned explicitly, e.g. Jason and Pollux (4.222-4.225).

Speaker: Boreads
Notes: In his own speech, given before Phineus’ speech in 4.474-4.484, Zetes already shows pity towards the seer (4.469-4.470).

Speaker: Jason/Boreads/Argonauts
Notes: Just after the Argonauts have left Phineus and set sails, however, fear of the Clashing Rocks arises (4.637-4.640).

Speaker: Argonauts
Notes: After Jason’s speech, the Argonauts also feel a sense of shame (4.655).

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Admiration is also an important component of Medea’s emotional state before Jason’s speech in 5.378-5.390 (cf. 5.374-5.375).

Speaker: Jason/Argonauts
Notes: Before the speech of Medea’s servant, only Jason is mentioned, afterwards, the group is referred to (5.426; not all of the Argonauts, but the scouting party, selected in 5.325-5.326).

Speaker: Aeetes
Notes: Aeetes, however, hides his anger through feigned friendliness (cf. 5.567-5.570).

Speaker: Juno
Notes: Juno is disguised as Medea’s sister Chalciope, but the emotions mentioned in the text are her authentic ones.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Jason’s reaction after Aeetes’ speech in 7.35-7.77 is a combination of different emotions: horror, sadness, anger, and astonishment (7.81-7.86).

Speaker: Juno
Notes: Juno’s emotional state after Venus’ speech in 7.172-7.186 is twofold, it comprises fear and hope (7.192).

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Before Venus-Circe gives her speech in 7.223-7.236, Medea is joyful about her “aunt’s” visit, but she also reproaches her for her long absence.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: Medea’s reaction to Venus-Circe’s speech also shows anger and horror (7.294-7.295).

Speaker: Venus
Notes: Before Medea’s speech in 7.385-7.387, Venus is compared to a mother bird that anxiously accompanies her fledglings that leave the nest for the first time (7.375-7.379). But the text is somewhat problematic, for the discussion and further references see Schirner 2023, 342 n. 1554.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: A significant component of Medea’s emotional state before and after Jason’s speech in 7.413-7.430 is also shame (7.411, 435); she is also called enamoured (7.412).

Speaker: Jason
Notes: Before Medea addresses Jason in 7.437-7.455, it is stated that Jason was just now humbly pleading Medea for help (7.431); in this speech, however, he is also reproachful (cf. 7.420-7.430).

Speaker: Jason
Notes: It is stated that Medea has cast some kind of love spell on Jason (7.488-7.489).

Speaker: Medea
Notes: In addition to infatuation, “sad shame” (aeger pudor, V. Fl. 7.514) is also an element of Medea’s emotional state after Jason’s speech in 7.490-7.509.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: In addition to infatuation, “sad shame” (aeger pudor, V. Fl. 7.514) is also an element of Jason’s emotional state before Medea’s speech in 7.516-7.521.

Speaker: Medea
Notes: This result (regarding Medea’s emotion after Jason’s speech) is obtained under the assumption that the reading trahit ridens (V. Fl. 7.531, “she pulls him away, laughing”) is the correct one. For this discussion and further references see Schirner 2023, 229-230.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: This result (regarding “emotion after the speech”) is obtained under the assumption that the conjecture miratur euntem (V. Fl. 8.55, “he admires her while she walks away”) instead of miseratur euntem (V. Fl. 8.55, “he feels sorry for her while she walks away”) is read. For this discussion and further references see Schirner 2023, 362-363.

Speaker: Colchians
Notes: In my interpretation, the wording in vultus micat undique terror (V. Fl. 8.333, “terror flashes across their faces from all sides”) describes the lightning as well as the effects it has on the Colchians; therefore, fear can be noted as “emotion before the speech”.

Speaker: Jason
Notes: With regard to “emotion after the speech”, shame is also an important component of Jason’s emotional state (cf. 8.464).
